metadata.summary: This modified Delphi consensus updates the definitions of MUSA ultrasound features used to describe adenomyosis. It distinguishes features that indicate ectopic endometrial tissue in the myometrium from features reflecting secondary myometrial changes, and addresses assessment of the junctional zone when diagnosis is uncertain. The document concerns sonographic recognition and description rather than treatment.

special_populations.considerations: Endometrial tissue extending into the myometrium requires cautious interpretation in this population: subendometrial lines and buds may indicate malignancy rather than adenomyosis.

conditions.name: adenomyosis
conditions.description: A benign uterine condition in which endometrial glands and stroma occur within the myometrium. Sonographic features are classified as direct signs of ectopic endometrial tissue or indirect signs of secondary myometrial changes.
conditions.epidemiology: Among women attending a gynecologic clinic, ultrasound identified adenomyosis in 34.5% of those seeking contraception counseling and 20.9% of those attending for other reasons, according to the cited studies.

subtypes.name: focal
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The lesion is localized rather than diffuse and may occur in the inner or outer myometrium, with or without surrounding myometrial hypertrophy.

subtypes.name: diffuse adenomyosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Myometrial involvement is diffuse; translesional vascularity is more likely in this form.

subtypes.name: adenomyoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Circumferential vascularity may occur. A large myometrial cyst may represent a cystic adenomyoma.

subtypes.name: adenomyosis limited to the outer myometrium
subtypes.distinguishing_features: This distribution may represent endometriosis extending into the uterus from outside.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: First-line imaging assessment for adenomyosis and its myometrial features.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited meta-analysis using histopathology of hysterectomy specimens as the reference standard reported sensitivity and specificity of 78% each. Direct features are myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands and echogenic subendometrial lines and buds. Indirect features are globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, irregular junctional zone and interrupted junctional zone. Indirect features without intramyometrial abnormalities do not establish the diagnosis; the diagnostic importance of each individual feature remains unknown.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the junctional zone in multiple planes and characterize changes that may be less apparent on two-dimensional imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly useful when the diagnosis remains uncertain; assessment may require specialized expertise.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal junctional zone suggests possible adenomyosis, whereas a regular, uninterrupted junctional zone indicates its absence. The experts favored assessment in sagittal, transverse and coronal planes. A cited meta-analysis reported an area under the receiver-operating-characteristics curve of 0.81 for an irregular junctional zone on 3D TVS. Junctional-zone thickness measurement currently has no clinical role, and no evidence-supported diagnostic cut-off was identified.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess myometrial features and whether the junctional zone can be visualized.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The junctional zone is interrupted if part of it cannot be seen in any plane on 2D or 3D transvaginal ultrasound. It is uninterrupted when clearly visible in all planes on either modality.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a direct sonographic feature of adenomyosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Round or oval cystic spaces within the myometrium count regardless of size; a hyperechogenic rim is not required. In cited studies, myometrial cysts had specificity of 86–98% and sensitivity of 47–55% for adenomyosis. Detectability of small cysts depends on ultrasound resolution.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a direct sonographic feature of adenomyosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These hyperechogenic myometrial areas have no connection to the endometrium and may have regular, irregular or poorly defined borders. No minimum diameter, number or distance from the endometrium applies. Echo enhancement can mimic this feature. Cited studies reported specificity of 78% and sensitivity of 51%.

diagnostic_workup.test: TVS assessment of echogenic subendometrial lines and buds
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a direct sonographic feature associated with endometrial tissue extending into the myometrium.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of the endometrial–myometrial interface.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The lines or buds may disrupt the junctional zone; the lines run approximately perpendicular to the endometrial cavity and remain continuous with the endometrium. Endometrial tissue entering the myometrium may indicate adenomyosis even without a line-like or bud-like appearance. In older and postmenopausal women, this finding requires caution because it might instead indicate malignancy. Cited studies reported specificity of 83–95.5% and sensitivity of 12–54%.

The myometrial serosa diverges from the cervix in at least two directions, while uterine corpus length, width and depth are approximately equal, producing a spherical contour. This describes shape rather than enlargement. Fibroids or an intracavitary abnormality can cause a false-positive appearance. Cited studies of women who underwent hysterectomy reported sensitivity of 51–74%.

diagnostic_workup.test: TVS assessment of asymmetrical myometrial thickening
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During comparison of anterior and posterior myometrial walls.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A thickness difference exceeding 5mm, or an anterior-to-posterior wall thickness ratio well above 1 or well below 1, is only a rule of thumb: no evidence-based cut-off is established. Different imaging planes, uterine rotation, transient contraction and fibroids can imitate asymmetry. Cited studies of women who underwent hysterectomy reported sensitivity of 23–62%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess fan-shaped shadowing behind a myometrial lesion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating this indirect sonographic feature.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Hypoechogenic stripes behind the lesion, sometimes alternating with hyperechogenic stripes, may be graded subjectively as slight, moderate or strong. Lateral edge shadows may instead suggest a fibroid or fibrosis associated with a Cesarean section scar. Assessment is best performed without color Doppler.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish myometrial cysts from blood vessels and help differentiate adenomyosis from fibroids.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a cystic space could be a vessel or when vascularity may clarify the nature of a lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Vessels crossing a lesion constitute translesional vascularity, which is more likely in diffuse adenomyosis and is not seen in fibroids according to the expert consensus. Circumferential vascularity may occur with an adenomyoma as well as around fibroids.

diagnostic_workup.test: TVS assessment of irregular junctional zone
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify an indirect feature when diagnostic uncertainty persists.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluation of the junctional zone could help clarify suspected adenomyosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cystic areas, hyperechogenic dots, buds or lines can produce irregularity. A high-quality image and assessment across multiple planes may help. Ultrasound measurement of junctional-zone thickness currently has no role in clinical practice.

diagnostic_workup.test: TVS assessment of interrupted junctional zone
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify an indirect feature when diagnostic uncertainty persists.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During assessment of the junctional zone on 2D or 3D transvaginal ultrasound.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Interruption means that some portion cannot be visualized in any plane. The proportion interrupted cannot be specified reliably as <50% or ≥50%. An abnormal junctional zone warrants scrutiny of the myometrium for direct features.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Serve as the reference standard in the diagnostic accuracy studies discussed.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The condition is defined by endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. The document notes that not all women with suspected adenomyosis undergo hysterectomy and that pathologists have no internationally agreed diagnostic criteria.

staging.additional_rules: No uniformly accepted or validated imaging-based system for diagnosing adenomyosis or classifying its severity is available.

recommendations.statement: Distinguish direct from indirect MUSA ultrasound features of adenomyosis. Classify myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands, and echogenic subendometrial lines and buds as direct features; classify globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, irregular junctional zone, and interrupted junctional zone as indirect features.
recommendations.context: Consensus statement from the third Delphi round.
recommendations.rationale: Direct features indicate ectopic endometrial tissue in the myometrium, whereas indirect features reflect changes secondary to that tissue.
recommendations.source_heading: General consensus points — Direct and indirect features of adenomyosis

recommendations.statement: Do not regard indirect ultrasound features alone as conclusive evidence of adenomyosis when intramyometrial abnormalities are absent.
recommendations.context: The specified intramyometrial abnormalities are myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands, and subendometrial lines or buds.
recommendations.rationale: Indirect features can occur without direct features, leaving the diagnosis uncertain.
recommendations.source_heading: General consensus points — Direct and indirect features of adenomyosis

recommendations.statement: When the diagnosis is uncertain, assess the junctional zone for irregularity in multiple planes using 3D ultrasound.
recommendations.rationale: Assessment of the junctional zone can help when the diagnosis is uncertain.
recommendations.source_heading: General consensus points — Assessment of junctional zone

recommendations.statement: Consider referral to a specialized gynecological practice for 3D ultrasound if the diagnosis remains uncertain.
recommendations.context: The technique may not be available in general gynecological practice.
recommendations.rationale: Evaluating the junctional zone across multiple planes with 3D ultrasound requires technical expertise.
recommendations.source_heading: General consensus points — Assessment of junctional zone

recommendations.statement: Interpret a regular, uninterrupted junctional zone as an indicator that adenomyosis is absent; an abnormal junctional zone on 3D ultrasound indicates possible adenomyosis.
recommendations.context: Consensus statements concerning the clinical relevance of the endometrial–myometrial JZ.
recommendations.source_heading: General consensus points — Assessment of junctional zone

recommendations.statement: Take myometrial cysts of any size into account as a direct feature of adenomyosis; neither a minimum nor a maximum size or a hyperechogenic rim is required.
recommendations.context: The revised feature describes rounded or oval cystic spaces within the myometrium.
recommendations.source_heading: Direct features of adenomyosis — Myometrial cysts

recommendations.statement: As a rule of thumb, use color Doppler to distinguish myometrial cysts from blood vessels.
recommendations.context: Assessment of the myometrial cyst feature.
recommendations.source_heading: Direct features of adenomyosis — Myometrial cysts

recommendations.statement: Identify hyperechogenic islands as hyperechogenic myometrial areas without a connection to the endometrium; do not require a minimum distance from the endometrium, diameter, or number of islands.
recommendations.context: The areas may be regular, irregular, or ill-defined.
recommendations.rationale: The experts considered a minimum distance from the endometrium arbitrary.
recommendations.source_heading: Direct features of adenomyosis — Hyperechogenic islands

recommendations.statement: Consider invasion of endometrial tissue into the myometrium a feature of adenomyosis even when it does not resemble echogenic subendometrial lines or buds.
recommendations.context: The experts retained the original definition of echogenic subendometrial lines and buds and added this diagnostic consideration.
recommendations.source_heading: Direct features of adenomyosis — Echogenic subendometrial lines and buds

recommendations.statement: Define a globular uterus by divergence of the myometrial serosa from the cervix in at least two directions rather than a course parallel to the endometrium, together with approximately equal measured diameters of the uterine corpus. Do not define this feature by uterine enlargement measurements.
recommendations.context: The directions may be anterior, posterior, or lateral. Fibroids or an intracavitary abnormality can produce a false-positive appearance.
recommendations.rationale: The term globular characterizes uterine shape rather than size.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Globular uterus

recommendations.statement: Use a difference in anterior and posterior myometrial wall thickness exceeding 5mm, or a thickness ratio well above 1 or well below 1, only as a rule of thumb for asymmetrical myometrial thickening; do not treat either as an evidence-based diagnostic cut-off.
recommendations.context: Different imaging planes, uterine rotation, myometrial contraction, and fibroids can complicate assessment.
recommendations.rationale: The experts found no evidence supporting a specific cut-off.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Asymmetrical myometrial thickening

recommendations.statement: Assess fan-shaped shadowing behind the myometrial lesion on grayscale images without color Doppler.
recommendations.context: The feature consists of hypoechogenic stripes that may alternate with linear hyperechogenic stripes. As a rule of thumb, shadows lateral to a lesion may instead suggest a fibroid or fibrosis associated with a CS scar.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Fan-shaped shadowing

recommendations.statement: Assess vascularity to help distinguish adenomyosis from fibroids and subendometrial cysts from blood vessels.
recommendations.context: As a rule of thumb, translesional vascularity is more likely with diffuse adenomyosis, whereas circumferential vascularity may occur with an adenomyoma.
recommendations.rationale: The experts distinguished vessels crossing a lesion from the vascular patterns observed with fibroids.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Translesional vascularity

recommendations.statement: For assessment of an irregular JZ, obtain a high-quality 2D or 3D still image of the area of interest; assessment in sagittal, transverse, and coronal planes with 3D ultrasound could also help.
recommendations.context: Consensus statement on assessment of irregular JZ.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Irregular junctional zone

recommendations.statement: Do not use ultrasound measurement of JZ thickness as a clinical diagnostic criterion for adenomyosis.
recommendations.context: The experts dismissed a proposed maximum-thickness measurement and did not endorse a diagnostic cut-off.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence for the clinical relevance of JZ thickness measurement was lacking.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Irregular junctional zone

recommendations.statement: Identify an interrupted JZ when part of it cannot be visualized in any plane on either 2D or 3D transvaginal ultrasound; consider it uninterrupted only when it is clearly visible in all planes on 2D ultrasound or in all planes on 3D ultrasound.
recommendations.context: Do not specify the interrupted proportion as <50% or ≥50%.
recommendations.rationale: The experts agreed that the proportion of the JZ that is interrupted cannot be specified.
recommendations.source_heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis — Interrupted junctional zone

artifacts.description: Round 1 assessed 15 videoclips; Round 2 assessed still images. Entries are n/N (%), median (interquartile range) or n (%). The prespecified consensus threshold was ≥66.7%. ‘Don’t know’ answers were omitted from agreement calculations. Total agreement represents the percentage of experts taking the same position on a proposed revision, either agreeing or disagreeing; it does not mean that every listed proposal was adopted. The results for several features in the table are inconsistent with the results stated elsewhere in the document; the final definitions appear in Table 3.
artifacts.summary: The table records agreement on identifying MUSA features and responses to proposed definition changes across the first two Delphi rounds. It distinguishes preliminary proposals from the later consensus definitions.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Variation in feature recognition, particularly for JZ findings, informs how cautiously these ultrasound findings should be interpreted. Proposed thresholds in this table must not be treated as final diagnostic criteria.

artifacts.title: Summary of general consensus statements agreed in Round 3 of modified Delphi procedure on definitions of Morphological Uterus Sonographic Assessment (MUSA) features of adenomyosis

rows: Distinction between direct and indirect features

Ultrasound features that are typical of adenomyosis are direct features, while ultrasound features that are a consequence of ectopic endometrium in the myometrium are indirect features. In the absence of intramyometrial abnormalities (myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands or subendometrial lines or buds), indirect features are not conclusive for the presence of adenomyosis. Currently, the importance of each individual ultrasound feature of adenomyosis is unknown. Prospective studies are needed to elucidate the clinical relevance of each individual feature. Direct features: cysts in the myometrium; hyperechogenic islands; echogenic subendometrial lines or buds. Indirect features: globular uterus; asymmetrical myometrial thickening; fan-shaped shadowing; translesional vascularity; irregular JZ; interrupted JZ.
Clinical relevance of endometrial–myometrial JZ

Although multiplanar assessment of the JZ in a 3D ultrasound volume is difficult technically, an abnormal JZ in 3D ultrasound images indicates possible adenomyosis. Referral to a specialized gynecological practice for 3D ultrasound might be useful if there is uncertainty about the diagnosis.
A regular, uninterrupted JZ is an indicator of absence of adenomyosis.

artifacts.description: The direct–indirect distinction is part of the Round 3 consensus. The table does not establish the diagnostic importance of any individual feature.
artifacts.summary: The table classifies ultrasound features as direct or indirect signs and describes how JZ findings affect diagnostic interpretation. It also addresses possible specialist referral when the diagnosis remains uncertain.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Indirect findings alone, without the listed intramyometrial abnormalities, are not conclusive for adenomyosis. JZ assessment may help resolve uncertainty but can require specialized 3D ultrasound expertise.

artifacts.title: Consensus on definitions of Morphological Uterus Sonographic Assessment (MUSA) features for diagnosing adenomyosis reached in Round 3 of modified Delphi procedure
artifacts.source_heading: Revision of definitions of MUSA features

rows: Myometrial cysts
Rounded lesions within the myometrium. Cystic contents may be anechoic, of low-level echogenicity, of ground-glass appearance or of mixed echogenicity. May be surrounded by a hyperechogenic rim.

Any size of myometrial cyst is relevant (no minimum or maximum size). Hyperechogenic rim is not obligatory. As a rule of thumb, color Doppler should be used to differentiate between blood vessels and myometrial cysts.
Rounded or oval cystic spaces of any size within the myometrium.
Hyperechogenic islands
Hyperechogenic areas within the myometrium that may be regular, irregular or ill-defined.

No minimum diameter and no minimum number of hyperechogenic islands are defined. Hyperechogenic islands should have no connection with the endometrium. There is no minimum distance from the endometrium.
Hyperechogenic areas within the myometrium that have no connection with the endometrium (no minimum distance, no minimum number). They may be regular, irregular or ill-defined.
Echogenic subendometrial lines and buds

Hyperechogenic subendometrial lines or buds may be observed disrupting the JZ. Hyperechogenic subendometrial lines are (almost) perpendicular to the endometrial cavity and are in continuum with the endometrium.
As a rule of thumb, any form of invasion of endometrial tissue into the myometrium is a feature of adenomyosis, even if its appearance is not that of lines or buds.
None.
Globular uterus
None.

This feature can be false positive in the presence of fibroids or intracavitary abnormality. No need to specify enlargement in terms of measurements because globular describes uterine shape, not size.

Globular uterus is present when the myometrial serosa diverges from the cervix in at least two directions (anterior/posterior/lateral), instead of following a trajectory parallel to the endometrium, and measured diameters (length/width/depth) of the uterine corpus are approximately equal. This results in the typical spherical shape of a globular uterus.
Asymmetrical myometrial thickening

The anterior and posterior myometrial walls are measured from the external uterine serosa to the external endometrial contour and should include the JZ but not the endometrium. The myometrial walls are measured in the sagittal plane, perpendicular to the endometrium. Both measurements are performed in the same plane, and the measurements should be obtained from the thickest point of the myometrial wall. The ratio between the anterior and posterior wall thickness is calculated. A ratio of around 1 indicates that the myometrial walls are symmetrical and a ratio well above or below 1 indicates asymmetry, although this may also be estimated subjectively.

There is no evidence-based cut-off to define asymmetry. Cut-off of ≥5mm difference in myometrial wall thickness, or ratio between the anterior and posterior wall thickness well above 1 or well below 1, should be used only as a rule of thumb. Caution: different planes/rotated uteri/myometrial contraction can imitate asymmetrical myometrial thickening.

As a rule of thumb only, asymmetrical thickening is present when the difference in thickness between the anterior and the posterior myometrial wall exceeds 5mm, or when the ratio between the anterior and posterior wall thickness is well above 1 or well below 1.
Fan-shaped shadowing
Presence of hypoechogenic linear stripes, sometimes alternating with linear hyperechogenic stripes. (The degree of shadowing is recorded subjectively as slight, moderate or strong.)

Fan-shaped shadowing should be present behind the myometrial lesion. As a rule of thumb, finding edge shadows lateral to the lesion might indicate the presence of a fibroid or fibrosis due to a CS scar rather than adenomyosis. This feature is best assessed in grayscale images without the use of color Doppler.

Presence of hypoechogenic stripes behind the myometrial lesion, sometimes alternating with linear hyperechogenic stripes (slight/moderate/strong). This feature is best assessed in grayscale images without the use of color Doppler.
Translesional vascularity
Translesional vascularity is characterized by the presence of vessels perpendicular to the uterine cavity/serosa crossing the lesion (hyperechogenic islands in the myometrium).

Assessing vascularity is helpful in discriminating between fibroids and adenomyosis, and between subendometrial cysts and blood vessels. As a rule of thumb, translesional vascularity is more likely to be present in diffuse adenomyosis, while circumferential vascularity may be present when there is an adenomyoma.
None.
Irregular JZ

The JZ can be irregular because of cystic areas, hyperechogenic dots, and hyperechogenic buds and lines. Magnitude of JZ irregularity: JZdif =JZmax −JZmin. Extent of JZ irregularity: percentage of JZ that is irregular (<50% or ≥50%, assessed subjectively).

Obtaining a high-quality 2D or 3D still image of the area of interest, and assessment in the sagittal, transverse and coronal planes using 3D ultrasound, could aid in the assessment of JZ. Ultrasound measurement of JZ thickness has currently no role in clinical practice.
The JZ can be irregular because of cystic areas, hyperechogenic dots, and hyperechogenic buds and lines. Ultrasound measurement of JZ thickness has currently no role in clinical practice.
Interrupted JZ
There is interruption of the JZ when a proportion of the JZ cannot be visualized (<50% or ≥50%, assessed subjectively).
It is impossible to specify what proportion (<50% or ≥50%) of the JZ is interrupted.

There is interruption of the JZ when a proportion of the JZ cannot be visualized on either 2D or 3D transvaginal ultrasound in any plane. An uninterrupted JZ means that the JZ is clearly seen in all planes on 2D ultrasound or in all planes on 3D ultrasound.

artifacts.description: The first definition column records the earlier MUSA consensus rather than the Round 3 revision. “None.” in the last column indicates that no replacement definition was proposed for that feature; the accompanying consensus statement remains relevant. The source groups the first 3 features as direct and the remaining 6 as indirect.
artifacts.summary: The table sets out the earlier wording, Round 3 consensus points and proposed updated definitions for all 9 MUSA features. It preserves cautions about mimicking findings and about thresholds that are only rules of thumb.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These definitions guide consistent ultrasound description and prevent preliminary thresholds from being mistaken for evidence-based diagnostic cut-offs.

document_sections.heading: CONTRIBUTION
document_sections.content: A modified Delphi procedure involving 13 specialists in ultrasound diagnosis of adenomyosis produced agreed revisions to the Morphological Uterus Sonographic Assessment (MUSA) feature definitions and separated those features into direct and indirect sonographic signs.

document_sections.heading: What are the novel findings of this work?
document_sections.content: The specialists reached consensus on updated descriptions of MUSA features of adenomyosis and on which features represent direct signs and which represent indirect signs.

document_sections.heading: What are the clinical implications of this work?
document_sections.content: The updated definitions and direct–indirect distinction should help clinicians recognize and diagnose adenomyosis. They also provide terminology for future investigations of associations between MUSA features, symptoms and reproductive outcomes.

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT
document_sections.content: The objective was to determine whether MUSA features of adenomyosis required clearer definitions and, where needed, agree on revisions. European gynecologists experienced in ultrasound diagnosis of adenomyosis took part in a modified Delphi procedure. In the first online round, they assessed nine previously described MUSA features in 15 two-dimensional (2D) transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) recordings; four recordings also contained three-dimensional (3D) still images. They commented on each feature’s presence or absence. In the second online round, they reviewed first-round results, proposed revisions and new 2D and 3D TVS still images. A third-round virtual meeting addressed the final definitions. Consensus had been set in advance at agreement by at least 66.7% of experts. Of 18 invitees, 16 agreed to participate; 11 completed and four partly completed the first round. The experts identified definitions needing greater detail and recommended 3D ultrasound to improve visualization of the junctional zone. In the second round, 15 experts reached agreement on feature presence or absence in most still images. Proposed revisions achieved consensus except those concerning echogenic subendometrial lines and buds and the interrupted junctional zone. At the final meeting, 13 experts agreed on revised definitions and on distinguishing direct signs, which indicate ectopic endometrial tissue within myometrium, from indirect signs, which reflect secondary myometrial changes. Myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands and echogenic subendometrial lines and buds were unanimously designated direct signs. Globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, irregular junctional zone and interrupted junctional zone were designated indirect signs.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: Adenomyosis is a benign uterine condition involving endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium. It may be focal or diffuse, affect inner or outer myometrium, and occur with or without adjacent myometrial hypertrophy. Disease confined to the outer myometrium may represent endometriosis extending inward from outside the uterus. Studies of women attending gynecologic clinics reported ultrasound diagnoses of adenomyosis in 34.5% of those seeking contraceptive counseling and 20.9% of those attending for other reasons. TVS is currently the first-line imaging approach. A cited meta-analysis using hysterectomy histopathology as the reference standard reported sensitivity and specificity of 78% each. The same source reported that 3D TVS may improve diagnostic accuracy by showing junctional-zone alterations in more detail than 2D ultrasound. No imaging-based system for diagnosis or severity classification has yet gained uniform acceptance or validation. The international MUSA group published sonographic terminology in 2015 and proposed a consistent approach to classification and reporting of disease morphology and extent in 2019. A cited pilot study found poor agreement between raters using MUSA features, whether their experience was high or moderate. Another study found good agreement between an expert and a trained non-expert for 2D-TVS images but poor agreement for 3D-TVS images. Unclear feature definitions may contribute to this variability. This study therefore sought to identify definitions needing clarification and obtain expert agreement on revisions through a modified Delphi procedure.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The investigators designed a three-round modified Delphi procedure to elicit collective expert opinion, not to conduct an interobserver agreement study. Two online questionnaire rounds used uterine ultrasound recordings and images from women suspected of having adenomyosis. These materials were intended to identify features with low agreement, gather suggestions for clearer definitions and assess agreement on revisions. A third round consisted of an online consensus meeting. Research Survey® questionnaires enabled participation across locations while reducing time and cost. The modified approach used expert comments to identify shared views and address disagreements. Educational and research images came from centers in Leuven and Amsterdam. Patients had undergone examinations by experienced gynecologists during specialist consultations at tertiary referral centers and were suspected of having adenomyosis on ultrasound. Equipment comprised a Voluson E8 Expert with a multifrequency (4–9MHz) endovaginal probe and a Samsung WS80A with a multifrequency (5–9-MHz) endovaginal probe. Eligible material had sufficient image resolution; eligible recordings showed sagittal and transverse uterine planes. Material showing another dominant condition, such as a uterine fibroid, uterine niche, deep endometriosis or malignancy, was excluded. The first author selected the images and recordings after 2years of supervised training in assessment of MUSA features during tertiary outpatient consultations. She did not serve as a Delphi panelist, although some gynecologists who had stored images did. The recordings and images contained no identifiable patient information. Three authors chose the nine features, drawing on two MUSA publications: globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial-wall thickening, myometrial cysts, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, hyperechogenic islands, echogenic subendometrial lines and buds, irregular junctional zone and interrupted junctional zone. Agreement percentages were calculated after each round. Two authors synthesized comments and returned them to the panel in the next round; experts did not know one another’s responses. Data collection ran from November 2018 to May 2020. The coordinating hospital’s ethics committee approved the study under nWMO 2018.669.

document_sections.heading: Expert panel recruitment
document_sections.content: Eligible panelists were gynecologists with demonstrable clinical experience in gynecologic ultrasound, participation in adenomyosis research and peer-reviewed international publications on the topic. Invitees could nominate other qualifying specialists. Invitations were not restricted by institution or country. Email invitations went to 18 prospective participants, and those accepting received an electronic questionnaire link.

document_sections.heading: Questionnaires to assess MUSA features of adenomyosis
document_sections.content: In round one, experts examined 15 ultrasound recordings; four included 3D still images. For each recording and each of the nine MUSA features, they indicated presence or absence using the four-point options ‘very sure’, ‘probably’, ‘probably not’ and ‘certainly not’, or selected ‘don’t know’ when unable to decide. They could comment throughout and were asked to explain ‘don’t know’ responses. The investigators also collected panelists’ country of residence, birth year, years as an ultrasound examiner, monthly number of patients examined by TVS and found to have adenomyosis, and number of adenomyosis-related journal articles or scientific-meeting presentations. In round two, the experts assessed a new set of 60 sagittal 2D-TVS still images and a separate set of 15 3D-TVS images, rather than volumes. The 3D presentations combined sagittal, transverse and rendered coronal views. For each feature with high first-round agreement, experts reviewed five to seven images; for features with low agreement, they reviewed 11 to 13. Still images ensured that every expert judged the same image. Experts answered ‘yes’ or ‘no’ about feature presence and could comment. Three authors developed proposed definition revisions from first-round comments. Panelists then indicated ‘yes’, ‘yes, with comment’ or ‘no, but instead: ...’ and could offer other revisions. Comments were prepared for the final meeting. The third round was a recorded virtual meeting on 8 May 2020. Its hosts presented earlier agreement results and proposed revisions, after which the experts discussed comments and further changes. A revised definition was considered agreed when every participating expert accepted it without further comment; if discussion did not achieve agreement, the feature was deemed to lack consensus.

document_sections.heading: Data analysis
document_sections.content: Questionnaire responses were summarized as n (%) or n/N (%). The advance consensus threshold was at least 66.7% of participating experts sharing a position on feature presence or absence, or agreeing with or rejecting a proposed revision. For proposed revisions, ‘yes’ and ‘yes, with comment’ counted together as agreement. First-round ‘don’t know’ replies were omitted from agreement calculations because they expressed no opinion. Earlier Delphi research had used thresholds between 51% and 80%, and a threshold of ≥66.7% had been used in previous studies. Analyses used IBM SPSS, version 20.0.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: Of 18 invited specialists, 16 participated and two did not answer the invitation. Participants came from seven countries. Median age was 43 (interquartile range (IQR), 40–58) years, and median gynecologist experience was 15 (IQR, 10–30) years. Most, 13/16, examined more than 10 women per month by TVS who were found to have adenomyosis, regardless of outpatient-clinic time. Eleven experts completed round one. Four started but did not finish: one evaluated two recordings, another nine and two others 10; one additional expert did not respond. In round one, agreement was reached for ≥80% of recordings for the presence of every MUSA feature. Median ‘don’t know’ responses were highest for irregular and interrupted junctional zone. Panelists frequently attributed assessment difficulty to insufficiently clear feature definitions, prompting proposed revisions for all features. Fifteen experts completed round two; the same expert absent from round one did not respond. Experts agreed on feature presence or absence in most images. For irregular junctional zone, agreement was reached in 3/6 (50%) 3D images and 4/5 (80%) 2D images; for interrupted junctional zone, the corresponding results were 3/8 (37.5%) and 4/4 (100%). Despite agreement on most image assessments, panelists agreed that definitions needed refinement. Round-two proposed revisions achieved consensus for globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, hyperechogenic islands and irregular junctional zone, but not for echogenic subendometrial lines and buds or interrupted junctional zone. Many experts requested direct–indirect classification. Thirteen specialists attended the virtual third round on 8 May 2020 and discussed classification, junctional-zone assessment and each feature definition. Table 1 summarizes agreement across the first two rounds; Tables 2 and 3 present the final general consensus points and feature definitions.

document_sections.heading: General consensus points
document_sections.content: The final meeting established general principles for classifying sonographic findings and assessing the junctional zone. Its agreed statements and definitions are summarized in Tables 2 and 3.

document_sections.heading: Direct and indirect features of adenomyosis
document_sections.content: Experts agreed to divide MUSA findings into direct and indirect signs. Direct findings indicate ectopic endometrial tissue within myometrium; indirect findings reflect consequences of that tissue, including muscular hypertrophy and sonographic artifacts. Direct signs comprise myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands and echogenic subendometrial lines or buds. Indirect signs comprise globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, irregular junctional zone and interrupted junctional zone. Without intramyometrial direct abnormalities, indirect signs do not establish adenomyosis conclusively. The importance of each individual sonographic feature is presently unknown, and prospective studies are needed to establish its clinical relevance.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of junctional zone
document_sections.content: The experts considered junctional-zone assessment useful when diagnosis is uncertain. A regular, uninterrupted junctional zone indicates absence of adenomyosis; an abnormal junctional zone on 3D images suggests that adenomyosis may be present. They suggested evaluating regularity in multiple planes using 3D ultrasound. They rejected measuring maximum junctional-zone thickness because evidence of its clinical relevance is lacking; sonographic thickness measurement currently has no clinical role. Multiplanar 3D assessment requires technical expertise and may not be available in general gynecologic practice. Referral to a specialized gynecologic service for 3D assessment might therefore be useful when the diagnosis remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Revision of definitions of MUSA features
document_sections.content: The specialists agreed on changes or additions to the descriptions of each MUSA feature. Table 3 sets out the earlier MUSA descriptions, final consensus statements and suggested definitions; no new definition was proposed there for echogenic subendometrial lines and buds or translesional vascularity.

document_sections.heading: Direct features of adenomyosis
document_sections.content: The three features classified as direct signs are myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands and echogenic subendometrial lines and buds. They indicate endometrial tissue within the myometrium.

document_sections.heading: Myometrial cysts
document_sections.content: Experts agreed on cyst presence in 14/15 first-round recordings and 6/7 second-round images. Comments highlighted uncertainty about very small cysts and size criteria. A revised proposal reached 80% agreement in round two. The earlier MUSA description allowed rounded intramyometrial lesions with anechoic, low-level echogenic, ground-glass or mixed contents and a possible hyperechogenic rim. Final consensus treats rounded or oval intramyometrial cystic spaces of any size as relevant: neither a minimum nor a maximum size or hyperechogenic rim is required. The experts recommended color Doppler to help distinguish cysts from vessels. All final-round experts classified myometrial cysts as a direct sign. Hyperechogenic islands were recognized in 13/15 first-round recordings and 9/13 second-round images. Experts warned that echo enhancement could resemble islands. They agreed that these intramyometrial hyperechogenic areas, whether regular, irregular or poorly defined, must not connect to the endometrium. They set no minimum distance from the endometrium, diameter or number, because such thresholds would be arbitrary. The final panel unanimously classified hyperechogenic islands as a direct sign representing ectopic endometrium.

document_sections.heading: Echogenic subendometrial lines and buds
document_sections.content: Presence of these findings reached consensus in 13/15 first-round recordings and 4/6 second-round still images. Assessment was hindered by absent 3D views, difficulty identifying the endometrial–myometrial interface and an invisible junctional zone. The original MUSA description concerned hyperechogenic subendometrial structures disrupting the junctional zone, with lines nearly perpendicular to the uterine cavity and continuous with the endometrium. In the final round, experts retained that definition and classified lines and buds as a direct sign. They additionally agreed that endometrial tissue entering the myometrium may indicate adenomyosis even when its shape does not resemble lines or buds.

document_sections.heading: Indirect features of adenomyosis
document_sections.content: The experts classified globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, irregular junctional zone and interrupted junctional zone as indirect signs. Such findings can occur without direct signs and, in that circumstance, do not settle the diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Globular uterus
document_sections.content: Experts agreed on this finding in 13/15 round-one recordings and 7/8 round-two still images. A proposed definition gained 86.7% agreement in round two and was accepted in round three. It describes myometrial serosa diverging from the cervix in at least two anterior, posterior or lateral directions rather than tracking parallel to the endometrium, with uterine-corpus length, width and depth approximately equal, producing a spherical form. ‘Globular’ describes shape rather than uterine size, so a measurement-based enlargement requirement was not adopted. Fibroids or intracavitary abnormalities can yield a false-positive appearance. All final-round experts categorized globular uterus as indirect.

document_sections.heading: Asymmetrical myometrial thickening
document_sections.content: Agreement on this sign occurred in 12/15 recordings in round one and 5/5 still images in round two. Experts found the absence of a metric definition challenging. The earlier MUSA approach measured anterior and posterior walls in the same sagittal plane, perpendicular to the endometrium, from outer serosa to outer endometrial contour, including the junctional zone but excluding the endometrium, at each wall’s thickest point. It compared wall thicknesses; a ratio around 1 indicated symmetry, whereas a ratio well above or below 1 suggested asymmetry, which could also be judged subjectively. Although 86.7% agreed in round two that a threshold was needed, the final group found no evidence-based cut-off and made no specific threshold recommendation. A difference of 5mm, or an anterior-to-posterior thickness ratio well above or well below 1, may be used only as a rule of thumb. Different imaging planes, uterine rotation, transient myometrial contraction and fibroids can mimic asymmetry. All final-round experts classified the feature as indirect.

document_sections.heading: Fan-shaped shadowing
document_sections.content: Feature assessment met the ≥66.7% agreement threshold in 12/15 first-round recordings and 9/9 second-round images. The original MUSA description concerned hypoechogenic linear stripes that can alternate with hyperechogenic stripes. Round-two experts agreed unanimously that the shadowing should lie behind a myometrial lesion, and round three accepted this criterion. The sign is best evaluated on grayscale images without color Doppler; its degree may be described as slight, moderate or strong. Edge shadows from fibroids or fibrosis associated with a Cesarean section scar can instead account for an appearance of shadowing. The group classified fan-shaped shadowing as indirect. For translesional vascularity, consensus on presence was reached in 13/15 first-round recordings and 4/5 second-round images. Experts questioned how to apply the term when no lesion was apparent. The existing MUSA definition describes vessels crossing a lesion perpendicular to the uterine cavity or serosa and was not revised. Round-two agreement was 80% for translesional vascularity being more likely in diffuse adenomyosis and 73.3% for circumferential vascularity being possible with adenomyoma. Although fibroids can contain vessels, the experts distinguished such vessels from vessels passing through a lesion and considered vascularity useful in distinguishing adenomyosis from fibroids and subendometrial cysts from blood vessels. They retained these vascular patterns as rules of thumb and classified translesional vascularity as indirect.

document_sections.heading: Irregular junctional zone
document_sections.content: Experts agreed on presence in 14/15 first-round recordings and, in round two, 3/6 of the 3D images and 4/5 of the 2D images. In 3/15 first-round recordings, ≥30% of raters chose ‘don’t know’. For the 11 recordings lacking 3D images, more than 50% of relevant comments cited difficulty evaluating the junctional zone without 3D ultrasound. The original MUSA description attributed irregularity to cystic areas, hyperechogenic dots, buds or lines, and described its magnitude as maximum minus minimum junctional-zone thickness and its extent as a subjective proportion of <50% or ≥50%. In round two, obtaining a high-quality still image of the relevant region gained 66.7% agreement as an aid; avoiding a diagnostic junctional-zone thickness cut-off gained 73.3%. In the final round, experts supported assessment with 3D-TVS across sagittal, transverse and coronal planes. They found no scientific evidence for recommending a junctional-zone thickness cut-off to diagnose adenomyosis, and thickness measurement currently has no clinical role. Irregular junctional zone was classified as indirect.

document_sections.heading: Interrupted junctional zone
document_sections.content: Presence reached consensus in 14/15 first-round recordings and, in round two, 3/8 3D images and 4/4 2D images. In 6/15 first-round recordings, ≥30% of experts selected ‘don’t know’. Panelists reported difficulty without 3D images, and no round-two proposed revision reached consensus. The earlier MUSA description defined interruption by nonvisualization of some junctional zone and suggested judging whether the proportion was <50% or ≥50%. In round three, experts agreed that this proportion cannot be specified reliably. Under the revised description, interruption means that some junctional zone cannot be seen in any plane on either 2D or 3D TVS; an uninterrupted junctional zone is clearly visible in every plane on 2D ultrasound or every plane on 3D ultrasound. Experts unanimously classified interruption as an indirect sign.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION Main findings
document_sections.content: The principal achievements were agreed revisions to MUSA feature descriptions and their classification as direct or indirect. That distinction reflects both disease pathology and the diagnostic implications of the signs: direct findings represent ectopic endometrial glands and stroma beyond the subendometrial layer, whereas indirect findings may occur without direct ones and then leave the diagnosis uncertain. Consistent application of the updated terminology could support more uniform detection, description and classification of adenomyosis. The experts considered junctional-zone assessment potentially important when diagnosis is uncertain and for research, while emphasizing its need for 3D ultrasound expertise.

document_sections.heading: Comparison with other studies
document_sections.content: Other imaging specialists have likewise treated myometrial cysts as direct signs and findings reflecting muscular hypertrophy as indirect. Direct signs can be subtle, and all three need not occur in one uterus. Because they represent endometrial tissue in myometrium, they are expected to be dependable indicators, although sensitivity is limited. Published diagnostic studies reported specificity of 86–98% for myometrial cysts, 83–95.5% for echogenic subendometrial lines and buds, and 78% for hyperechogenic islands; corresponding sensitivities were 47–55%, 12–54% and 51%, respectively. Indirect signs may be easier to see, particularly as disease and muscular hypertrophy progress. Their apparent prevalence therefore depends on the population examined. Recognition, especially of junctional-zone features, likely varies with examiner experience, equipment, 3D-TVS availability and ability to obtain and interpret 3D volumes. Cited work reported better recognition with greater expertise. Among studies of women undergoing hysterectomy, reported sensitivities varied from 23–62% for asymmetric myometrial walls and 51–74% for globular uterus; differences in disease severity and ultrasound expertise may explain that variation. Fibroids can also produce asymmetry or a globular appearance. This study did not assess how well either sign separates adenomyosis from other conditions; such discrimination remains a subject for future study with updated MUSA terminology.

document_sections.heading: Remarks on junctional zone, cysts in the myometrium, and hyperechogenic lines and buds
document_sections.content: Expert agreement about irregular or interrupted junctional zone was poorer than for the other adenomyosis features. A cited meta-analysis reported a pooled receiver-operating-characteristics area of 0.81 for diagnosis using irregular junctional zone on 3D TVS; the experience of examiners in the underlying studies may explain that performance. Rasmussen etal. reported better agreement on irregular and interrupted junctional zone among highly experienced raters than among moderately experienced raters. Reliability of 3D uterine assessment may improve as expertise grows. This panel considered multiplanar 3D TVS essential for properly viewing the junctional zone, yet previously reported poor intra- and interobserver agreement among moderately experienced examiners limits the diagnostic usefulness of an abnormal junctional zone in general gynecologic practice. An irregular, interrupted or invisible junctional zone suggests possible adenomyosis and should lead the examiner to inspect the myometrium closely for direct signs. Whether junctional-zone assessment improves patient management when diagnosis is uncertain needs study; referral to specialist gynecologic practice might be required. In older and postmenopausal women, endometrial tissue entering the myometrium warrants caution because apparent subendometrial lines and buds might indicate malignancy rather than adenomyosis. Ultrasound spatial resolution limits the smallest detectable intramyometrial cyst, and a large cyst may be a cystic adenomyoma. Nevertheless, the panel agreed that cysts of any size should count when assessing this MUSA feature.

document_sections.heading: Strengths and limitations
document_sections.content: The modified Delphi design allowed expert comments to expose disagreements and shape revised definitions. Participation across different clinical and research environments increased the potential diversity of views; a minimum of 12 participants is generally accepted for a consensus effort. Panel selection remains a limitation: no radiologists participated, the panel did not encompass all international experts, and participants represented nine institutions in seven European countries, including four from one institution. Of those four, only two managed the project and attended the final consensus meeting. The expertise criteria may be considered arbitrary. Not all experts joined every round or completed every first-round recording. Consequently, recordings differed in numbers of assessors and ‘don’t know’ responses, so agreement calculations used different denominators. The study was not designed to measure interobserver agreement or diagnostic accuracy; agreement results served only to direct discussion about definitions. Online presentation reduced image resolution. Ideally, 3D TVS would be reviewed as operator-manipulable volumes on a high-end device. The authors speculate that poorer image quality and inability to manipulate volumes probably lowered agreement for 3D junctional-zone images. Although recordings are preferable for image assessment, round two used still images so that all experts judged identical material.

document_sections.heading: Future perspectives
document_sections.content: Clearly specified ultrasound findings are needed for diagnoses useful to clinicians and researchers. Further intra- and inter-rater reliability studies should examine direct and indirect MUSA signs, particularly junctional-zone findings, with sufficiently trained raters of differing experience. A Delphi exercise including radiologists could test the updated definitions in a broader expert panel. A few previous studies examined relationships between adenomyosis ultrasound findings and clinical outcomes, but only one referred to MUSA definitions. Further work should evaluate how the presence, number, size and location of direct and indirect features—including their relation to the junctional zone and the uterine layers affected—relate to symptoms. Diagnostic accuracy for one or more direct or indirect features also needs investigation. Such studies are difficult because hysterectomy is the reference standard, not every woman with suspected adenomyosis undergoes hysterectomy, and pathologists lack international agreement on diagnostic criteria.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The article updates the ultrasound terminology and definitions first presented by MUSA in 2015, based on consensus among 13 gynecologists experienced in sonographic diagnosis of adenomyosis. The updated approach distinguishes direct from indirect signs. Prospective studies are needed to establish associations of these signs—and disease location, extent and size—with symptoms and treatment outcomes. Using consistent MUSA terminology should make future study results easier to compare.

document_sections.heading: RESUMEN
document_sections.content: The Spanish-language abstract restates the study objective, three-round modified Delphi design, advance consensus threshold of 66,7%, participation of 16 of 18 invited specialists, and final discussion among 13 experts. It repeats the recommendation to use 3D ultrasound to improve junctional-zone visualization and the distinction between direct signs of ectopic endometrial tissue and indirect signs of secondary myometrial change. It identifies myometrial cysts, hyperechogenic islands and echogenic subendometrial lines and buds as direct signs, and globular uterus, asymmetrical myometrial thickening, fan-shaped shadowing, translesional vascularity, irregular junctional zone and interrupted junctional zone as indirect signs.
